title: Alphabets, strings, formal languages — and the notation that costs points
summary: Define alphabet, string, language in Chen's words; compute lengths, exponents, reverses, prefixes; tell λ, ϕ, {λ} apart; translate English ↔ set-builder for 'at least / exactly / starts with' languages and their complements; compute L₁L₂ and Lⁿ with independent indices.
sourceNote: Lesson 3 (Aug 31) and Lesson 4 (Sep 2) slides + appendix, Assignment 2 and 3 solution keys.

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **The idea** In this course a *language* is not English. It's a **set of strings** — any set of strings. {ab, aabb, aaabbb, …} is a language. Why care? Because every yes/no question about text can be rewritten as 'is this string in that set?' *Is this a valid email?* → is it in the set of valid emails. *Does this program compile?* → is it in the set of well-formed programs. So 'which languages can a machine recognize' is the same question as 'which problems can a machine solve'. Strings and languages are the vocabulary for asking that.
blocks.slide: A language is a yes/no problem in disguise

blocks.body: **The four branches (a 2-point question on Assignment 2)** The theory of computation has four branches: **Formal Languages**, **Automata**, **Computability**, **Complexity**. 0.5 points each. It will come back.
a **nonempty, finite set of symbols**. Symbols are indivisible. His 'celebrity alphabet' is Σ = {a, b}.
a **finite sequence of symbols from Σ**. It need not mean anything. Strings are named w (then u, v, then x, y, z).
the number of symbols. |babba| = 5.
the string with zero symbols. |λ| = 0. λ can never be a *symbol* in an alphabet (λaabb would be ambiguous).

rows: the empty **set** — a language with no strings
the empty **string** — a string with no symbols
a language with **one** string, the empty one
blocks.slide: The three empties — never confuse them

blocks.title: Exponent, the a⁰ trap, and reverse

frames.caption: **Exponent** on a string: wⁿ means n copies of w glued together (concatenated).
Three copies of ab. Length multiplies: |wⁿ| = |w| · n.

lines: zero copies of anything = the empty string
frames.caption: Zero copies is the string with no symbols: **λ** (lambda), the empty string. |λ| = 0. This is the string-world cousin of the empty set, and they are *not* the same thing.

lines: the exponent applies only to the last symbol
frames.caption: Trap: without parentheses the exponent belongs to just the symbol before it. aaba⁰ = aab, but (aaba)⁰ = λ. Quiz question every year.
The pattern you'll see most: aᵐbᵐ. Same count of a's and b's, all a's first. This is the shape of the 'celebrity language' in the next section.
**Reverse** flips the order of symbols. Reversing a concatenation reverses each piece *and* swaps their order. A **palindrome** is a string with wᴿ = w (abba).

blocks.body: write u then v. |uv| = |u| + |v|. λ is the neutral element: λw = wλ = w.
a run of consecutive symbols. If w = uv, then u is a **prefix** and v a **suffix**. Both λ and w itself count as prefixes and suffixes.

(Sigma star): every string of zero or more symbols from Σ — including λ. **Σ⁺**: one or more — excluding λ. Both are infinite. Σ⁺ = Σ∗ − {λ}. Σ∗ is 'the universal language over Σ' — every language over Σ is a subset of it.

blocks.title: Listing every split
blocks.body:
List all (prefix, suffix) pairs of w = abaaba.

1. A split is a place to cut. With 6 symbols there are 7 cut positions (before the first, between each pair, after the last).
2. (λ, abaaba), (a, baaba), (ab, aaba), (aba, aba), (abaa, ba), (abaab, a), (abaaba, λ).
3. Always |w| + 1 pairs. Don't forget the two ends.

blocks.answer: {a, 1} yes. { } no — must be nonempty. {ab} yes — here 'ab' is one indivisible symbol. {λ} no — λ can't be a symbol.
2 (λ adds nothing). λ. ab (only the last a is raised to 0). λ.

blocks.body: **♥ Definition (2 points on Assignment 2)** **A formal language over Σ is any subset of Σ∗.** A language is a set, so everything from Lesson 1 applies (union, complement, subset…). Named L. Two special ones: the **empty language** ϕ, and the **λ-language** {λ}.

blocks.md: L = { aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 0 } = {λ, ab, aabb, aaabbb, …}: some a's, then *the same number* of b's. Compare { aⁿbᵐ | n, m ≥ 0 }: any number of a's, then any number of b's — n and m are independent, so aab is in it but not in the first. That one letter of difference is the whole distinction between what a DFA can and cannot do (Lesson 12).

frames.caption: **Concatenation of languages**: L₁L₂ = { uv | u ∈ L₁, v ∈ L₂ } — take a string from L₁, then a string from L₂, glue them, and do that for *every* pair. It's a Cartesian product where you concatenate instead of making tuples.
x followed by m; x followed by n.
L₁L₂ = {xm, xn, ym, yn, zm, zn}. Six strings, |L₁| · |L₂|. In general |L₁L₂| **≤** |L₁|·|L₂| — ≤, not =, because two different pairs can glue into the same string (a·ab = aa·b).

lines: ϕL = Lϕ = ϕ      (like × 0: no strings to pick from)
frames.caption: Two special cases he asks about. Concatenating with the empty *language* gives the empty language — there's no string in ϕ to pick. Concatenating with {λ} — a language whose only string is the empty string — changes nothing.

lines: L² = LL = { aⁿbⁿ aᵐbᵐ | n, m ≥ 0 }
frames.caption: **Exponent on a language** concatenates it with itself. The two copies choose their n *independently* — so the second copy needs its own variable m. aabb·ab ∈ L² with n = 2, m = 1. Also: L⁰ = {λ} for every L, even ϕ⁰ = {λ}.

blocks.body: Lᴿ = { wᴿ | w ∈ L }. { aⁿbⁿ }ᴿ = { bⁿaⁿ }.
L₁L₂ = { uv | u ∈ L₁, v ∈ L₂ }. ϕL = ϕ. {λ}L = L.
n copies concatenated, each with its own index. L⁰ = {λ}, even for ϕ.

blocks.md: - Set operations as usual. **Complement** L̄ = Σ∗ − L — the universal set is Σ∗.

blocks.prompt: L = { cⁿdⁿ | n ≥ 0 }. Write L² and Lᴿ.
blocks.answer: L² = { cⁿdⁿcᵐdᵐ | n, m ≥ 0 } (independent indices, not c²ⁿd²ⁿ). Lᴿ = { dⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 0 }.

sections.heading: English ↔ set-builder: the patterns he expects

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **How to write 'at least one a'** Assignment 3 asked for languages in set-builder and their complements, and the key wants specific shapes. The trick for all of them: describe the string as a *template* — some free stuff, the thing you require, more free stuff — where 'free stuff' is bⁿ (only b's) or w ∈ Σ∗ (anything). 'At least one a' becomes: any b's, then an a, then anything: { bⁿaw | n ≥ 0, w ∈ Σ∗ }. Once you see the template idea, the whole table writes itself.

rows: { bⁿ | n ≥ 0 } — no a at all
{λ, a} ∪ { aaw | w ∈ Σ∗ } ∪ { bw | w ∈ Σ∗ }
strings containing at least one b
at least n / at most n

blocks.title: Complement by asking 'how can a string fail?'
blocks.body:
L = { aⁿb | n ≥ 0 } over {a, b}: some a's then exactly one b at the end. Write L̄.

1. A string is *not* in L in exactly two ways. Way 1: it has no b at all — just a's (including λ): { aⁿ | n ≥ 0 }.
2. Way 2: it has a b, but the b isn't the last symbol — something follows it: { aⁿbw | n ≥ 0, w ∈ Σ⁺ }. (Σ⁺, not Σ∗, because if w were λ the string would be in L.)
3. Union the two ways.
blocks.slide: Assignment 3 Q1: the complement of { aⁿb | n ≥ 0 }

blocks.title: Assignment 2 Q12: roster form of { w@w | w ∈ {a,b}∗ }

lines: pattern: some string w, then @, then the SAME w again
frames.caption: Assignment 2 Q12: write this in roster form. Read the pattern first. The variable w appears twice, so both halves are identical.
Smallest w first. w = λ (the empty string, allowed because of the ∗): λ@λ is just **@**. Note that the string is '@', not λ — the @ is always there. Including λ in the roster was a −0.5 deduction.
Length-2 w's, then it goes on forever. Infinite language, so the roster must end with '…' (−0.25 if missing).

lines: L = { @, a@a, b@b, aa@aa, ab@ab, ba@ba, bb@bb, … }
frames.caption: The accepted answer. Deductions from the key: no braces −0.25 · no '…' −0.25 · λ included −0.5 · halves don't match (a@b) −1 · anything else −1.5.

blocks.prompt: Over Σ = {a, b}, write 'more than one a' and its complement in set-builder.
blocks.answer: L = { bⁿabᵐaw | n, m ≥ 0, w ∈ Σ∗ } (two a's guaranteed, anything after). Complement = zero or one a: { bⁿ | n ≥ 0 } ∪ { bⁿabᵐ | n, m ≥ 0 }.

blocks.md: Every one of these is a deduction from the Assignment 1–3 keys. Assignment 2 lost 7.5 of 24 points, almost all on these. Write them on a card and check every quiz answer against the card before submitting — it's the cheapest grade recovery in any of your classes.

blocks.body: Sets and languages get braces { }; tuples get parentheses ( ).
λ is the empty *string*; ϕ or { } is the empty *set*; {λ} is a language with one string.
In set-builder, comma = *and*. Write 'or' (or ∨) for or.
Always name the alphabet: 'over Σ = {a, b}'.
Roster form of an infinite language ends with '…'.
Strings are w, u, v; languages are L; alphabets are Σ.
Complement of a language means Σ∗ − L; you need Σ.
w⁰ = λ (a string), but L⁰ = {λ} (a language).
Exponents on languages create *independent* indices (n, m).
A ⊂ B (proper) requires A ≠ B; when in doubt, ⊆.
Roster elements separated by commas, inside one pair of braces.
Don't invent notation. If the slide wrote it a certain way, write it that way.

blocks.md: **Lessons 3–4 in one breath.** Σ is a finite nonempty set of symbols; a string is a finite sequence of them; Σ∗ is all strings; a language is any subset of Σ∗. Strings concatenate, reverse, and take exponents (w⁰ = λ); languages do too (L⁰ = {λ}, independent indices). Complement is relative to Σ∗. Three empties: ϕ, λ, {λ}. Templates like bⁿaw turn English into set-builder.

exercises.title: String arithmetic
exercises.prompt: Let u = ab, v = ba. Compute: (a) |uvu|, (b) (uv)ᴿ, (c) u³, (d) uv⁰, (e) (uv)⁰, (f) the number of (prefix, suffix) pairs of uvu.
hints: Concatenate first, then apply the operation to the result. Write the actual strings out — don't do it symbolically.
(d) vs (e) is the aaba⁰ trap: without parentheses the exponent applies only to v. And in (f), λ and the whole string both count.
(b): reverse of a concatenation = reverse each part and swap the order. Check it by writing uv out and reading it backwards.
solution: (b) uv = abba; reversed = abba (it's a palindrome). Via the rule: vᴿuᴿ = ab·ba = abba ✓.
exercises.why: String operations are the primitives of every parser, every regex engine, and every 'does this input match this format' check. Getting the empty string right is what stops off-by-one bugs at the ends of inputs.

exercises.title: English → set-builder, plus complements
exercises.prompt: Over Σ = {a, b}, write in set-builder: (a) strings that end in b; (b) strings with exactly two a's; (c) strings of even length. Then write the complement of (a) and (b).
hints: Use templates: 'free stuff' is w ∈ Σ∗ (anything) or bⁿ (only b's). Put the required part where it must be and free stuff around it.

Chen's deductions: missing 'over Σ', missing the condition on n, and — for (b) — forgetting that between and around the two a's there can be b's *but not a's*. { w a w a w | w ∈ Σ∗ } is wrong (the w's could contain a's).
For complements, ask 'how does a string fail?'. (a) fails if it's empty OR ends in a. (b) fails if it has fewer than 2 a's OR more than 2.
solution: (a) { wb | w ∈ Σ∗ }. Complement: {λ} ∪ { wa | w ∈ Σ∗ }.
(b) { bⁿ a bᵐ a bᵏ | n, m, k ≥ 0 }. Complement: { bⁿ | n ≥ 0 } ∪ { bⁿ a bᵐ | n, m ≥ 0 } ∪ { w | w ∈ Σ∗, w has at least three a's } — or { bⁿabᵐabᵏaw | n,m,k ≥ 0, w ∈ Σ∗ } for the last piece.
(c) { w | w ∈ Σ∗, |w| is even } — or { uv | u, v ∈ Σ∗, |u| = |v| }. Note λ ∈ this set (length 0 is even).
exercises.why: Translating a plain-English requirement into a precise pattern — and then writing what *doesn't* match — is the core of writing validators, firewall rules, and test cases. The complement is the part people skip, and it's where the security holes are.

exercises.title: Grade it like Chen
exercises.prompt: A student answers the question 'Write L = { aⁿb | n ≥ 0 } in roster form' with: `(λ, b, ab, aab, aaab)`. List every deduction the key would take and write the correct answer.

choices.text: Only one thing is wrong: the brackets.
choices.feedback: The brackets are wrong, but keep looking — is λ actually in L? And is the language finite?

choices.text: Three things: brackets, λ shouldn't be there, and it's missing '…'.
choices.feedback: Right. Parentheses instead of braces (−0.25 to −0.5), λ included when n = 0 gives 'b' not λ (−0.5), and no '…' for an infinite language (−0.25).

choices.text: Nothing — λ is in L because n can be 0.
choices.feedback: n = 0 gives a⁰b = λb = b. The string is b, not λ. The b is always there.

hints: Check three things every time: the brackets, whether the smallest element is right, and whether the list needs '…'.
The λ trap: a⁰ is λ, but a⁰b is b. Plug n = 0 in fully before writing the first element.
Chen's rule 5: roster form of an infinite language ends with '…'. Rule 1: sets get braces.
solution: Brackets: a set needs { }, not ( ). Deduction.
First element: n = 0 → a⁰b = b, not λ. λ ∉ L. Deduction.
Correct: L = { b, ab, aab, aaab, … }.
exercises.why: Reading your own answer the way a strict grader would is a skill in itself — it's code review applied to yourself. In this class it's worth about a third of the points you've been losing.
